newsitem.title: THAILAND: INTERVIEW - Thailand wants more oil refineries.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Thailand wants more oil refineries.

text.p: Thailand wants to attract more oil refineries after financial barriers affecting their operations are scrapped, Industry Minister Korn Dabbaransi said on Wednesday.

He told Reuters that the cabinet will soon approve a proposal to remove requirements for a two percent royalty and a signature bonus of 350-million baht ($15.3 million) payment on oil refineries to further liberalise the domestic oil industry.
The old levy system will be replaced by excise taxes which would be fairer, he said.

"The move will create an equal and level playing field for all refineries and open the gate for new ones to enter. Thailand wants more refineries. My philosophy is oil supplies should exceed demand to benefit consumers," he said.
"It is not for me to decide if the plan will make the competition tougher. Let investors decide on that based on market conditions," he added.
Thai oil refineries face different levies which have long been a subject of complaints among players in the industry.

Thai Oil, Thailand's largest oil refiner, is subject to a tax and profit sharing scheme, Bangchak Petroleum is only subject to normal business taxation, while newcomers like Rayong Refinery and Star Petroleum had to pay a 350-million baht signature bonus and two percent royalty based on production.
"Your factories do not have to be categorised as refineries. It can be a condensate splitter, or anything. As long as it produces oil, you have to pay excise tax," he said.

Korn said he will push for state-run Petroleum Authority of Thailand to build its own refinery as soon as possible. PTT is expected to submit a plan to build a 300,000 barrel-per-day refinery, or more, for approval within this year.

Although PTT holds shares in various refineries, it does not have one of its own. The government wanted the agency to be fully integrated before it becomes privatised and that would occur in the next two-three years.

Sukhothai Petroleum will begin building its 20-billion baht 120,000-barrel-per-day oil refinery in the southern Songkhla province by the end of this year. The construction is expected to be completed by 1999.
Thailand currently has five refineries with combined capacity of 777,000 barrels per day.
Korn said rising supplies would also ease oil smuggling problems. Industry estimates put the volume of smuggled oil, mostly diesel, last year as high as 50,000 barrels per day.
"More supplies will cut down the amount needed to be imported and make smuggling less attractive," he said.
